architecture.title: How this site works
architecture.lede: A hiring manager's tour of the machine: what runs where, what the model is allowed to decide, and what stops it.
architecture.pitch: One Next.js deploy holds a static site, a text console and the brain of a voice agent. ElevenLabs handles the audio; every word the agent says comes from a prompt I compiled from my own CV and project notes, and passes a guard before it reaches you.

flow.s1: The browser asks for a session. No token is minted until a live microphone track exists.
flow.s2: ElevenLabs opens a WebRTC session, transcribes your speech and calls my own LLM endpoint.
flow.s3: That endpoint builds a byte-identical system prompt, adds a small dynamic note, and streams from DeepSeek with Claude Haiku as failover.
flow.s4: A guard reads the stream before it is spoken. A blocked answer is replaced by a fixed refusal, not rewritten.
flow.s5: Tool calls only change what the page shows. Nothing is emailed, downloaded or stored until you click a form yourself.

architecture.prompt: The knowledge lives in a private repo as structured files: facts, proof points with metrics, project notes with a public level, stories, red lines and a denylist. A build step validates them, compiles one system prompt and fails the build if a forbidden field exists at all — the logistics schema is strict, so a salary key cannot be added by accident.
architecture.notAllowedTitle: What the model is not allowed to decide

notAllowed.n1: Who receives an email. Recipients are fixed in code; the model can only open a form.
notAllowed.n2: Any phone number, or any email other than the one contact address.
notAllowed.n3: Any salary figure, range or rate.
notAllowed.n4: Anything about employers beyond what I compiled into the corpus.
notAllowed.n5: Whether I am job hunting. The phrase is always "open to conversations".

architecture.arabic: The Arabic side speaks Masri, the dialect I actually speak, not Modern Standard Arabic. That is enforced in three places: the persona and few-shot examples in the corpus, a normaliser that fixes numerals and Latin runs before speech, and an eval set graded by a judge model plus native speakers.
architecture.evals: Every prompt change runs an eval suite before it can ship: red-line cases that must refuse, dialect cases graded for Masri, and grounding cases that must cite the corpus. Guardrail tests run in CI and block the deploy.
architecture.privacy: Audio is never stored by me. Transcripts are pseudonymised with a daily-salted hash and deleted after 30 days. Voice minutes are capped in Postgres — counted from rows, never from process memory — with a kill switch and a spend ceiling.
architecture.change: Sending text to a model hosted in China is the sharpest trade-off here, and it is disclosed on the privacy page. If the dialect quality holds on a model with a European or US home, that is the first thing I move.
